author: janleike
text:
This is the most important plot of alignment lore:

Whenever you optimize a proxy, you make progress on your true objective for a while.

At some point you start overoptimizing and do worse on your true objective (hard to know when).

This applies to all proxy measures ever. https://t.co/XToScPGqIv

text: @SpencrGreenberg @KerryLVaughan Everyone in the world would need to stop at the same time. And where exactly is the line with narrow AI? Do we stop building AI altogether? And how do we check that no one cheats?

text: @ahron_maline Yup that's the main idea

author: janleike
text: @ahron_maline For this to work, you'd need the assistance to be at least as smart as the main agent and have a bunch of advantages over it (more information, longer thinking time, access to the main agent's internals, ...)

author: janleike
text:
@ahron_maline This is definitely a concern! We're advocating for using AI to defend against this: AI assistance during supervision can point out attempts at deception.

In the paper we have some experiments on misleading answers with subtle flaws written by humans. Our models help find them.

author: janleike

author: janleike
text:
In this paper, we work with summarization and a few toy tasks, which aren't actually that hard for humans.

Plus, our language models aren't smarter than humans.

Yet our models can already meaningfully help evaluation.

author: janleike
text:
Why is this a big deal?

To align superhuman models with human intent, humans need to understand what they are doing, especially when the task is difficult.

This is the main idea behind recursive reward modeling and other scalable alignment approaches:

https://t.co/TNNMlxTC2q

Usually, but not always, it's a decent proxy because happy users lead to profits.

text: @scottniekum Arguably that there is a difference from how performance is often measured: using a set of fixed benchmarks. We use humans in the loop for training and eval because we want to get closer to human preferences. But you could also call this sort of eval "another performance metric."

author: janleike
text: @scottniekum I'd be excited about progress on (probabilistic) guarantees! This is not something we set out to do here; we did a much simpler thing and evaluated how well it works. Hopefully we'll have better techniques in the future.

author: janleike
text: @scottniekum We certainly didn't want to claim that what we were doing in this paper is the only way to approach alignment. There is a lot to do and it's a large space with lots of different approaches! Hopefully at some point we'll only train aligned models, without an intermediate step.

author: janleike

author: janleike
text: To me, one of the most surprising bits was that our model, InstructGPT, learned to generalize following instructions and does so even in foreign language and code, where we don't really supervise it.

author: janleike
text: For comparison: We spent <2% of the pretraining compute on fine-tuning and collect a few 10,000s of human labels and demos. Our 1.3b parameter models (GPT-2 sized!) are preferred over a prompted 175b parameter GPT-3.

author: janleike
text:
Disclaimer: There isn't really much new in terms of methods or algorithms.

But it shows that our alignment techniques work in a real-world setting.

This is cheaper and more effective at making a more useful model than just making it bigger.

In the experiments almost all mistakes were made by humans. But: the technique still works just as well if we only train on the safe demonstrations.

This is an important proof of concept that this technique scales and that the goal of zero safety violations is achievable!

author: janleike
text:
How do you train an RL agent to avoid unsafe states, without knowing where they are?

Answer: ask humans about hypotheticals.

Exciting progress, with colleagues at DeepMind: training agents in 3D environments without ever falling off a cliff!
